target: AG1’s claim that alternative energy can effectively replace fossil fuels because some countries have high renewable electricity shares and the U.S. has historically remained below 20% alternative energy.
objection: High renewable performance in a few countries does not prove that alternatives have broadly and reliably displaced fossil fuels in large, ongoing energy systems. AG2 argues that the U.S. historical ceiling on alternative energy use shows scaling has been limited, so the transition has not yet been demonstrated at broad system level.

target: AG1’s claim that alternative energies can replace fossil fuels in the whole energy system.
objection: AG2 objects that the evidence cited is mostly about electricity, while fossil fuels are also heavily used in transportation and in industrial/building heat. Because those sectors require large-scale electrification or new fuels and infrastructure, high renewable electricity shares alone do not show that fossil fuels can be eliminated across the whole energy system.

target: AG2’s inference that because U.S. alternative energy has never exceeded about 20%, alternatives have not effectively replaced fossil fuels in large systems.
objection: That inference is too narrow because other countries already run large grids with very high fossil-fuel displacement. AG1 points to Iceland, Paraguay, Costa Rica, and Norway as counterexamples showing that the U.S. historical trajectory is not a valid basis for denying that alternatives can effectively replace fossil fuels.

target: AG1’s assumption that alternative energy can provide the firm, dispatchable power needed for grids without fossil-fuel backstops.
objection: AG2 argues that large grids still need firm, dispatchable supply during low-renewable periods and peak demand. Until alternatives can reliably provide that firmness at scale, fossil fuels remain the practical backstop, making full replacement unrealistic without a bridge fuel such as natural gas.

target: AG2’s claim that alternative energy cannot provide firm, dispatchable grid-scale power.
objection: AG1 replies that this reliability objection is already contradicted by real-world systems. Iceland relies on geothermal, Norway on reservoir hydropower, and Paraguay and Costa Rica also operate at very high renewable shares, showing that alternative energy can already supply the firmness needed for reliable grids.

target: AG1’s broader claim that high renewable electricity shares prove fossil fuels can be replaced broadly and reliably.
objection: AG2 repeats that electricity decarbonization is not the same as eliminating fossil fuels across all sectors. Transportation fuels and industrial/building heat still depend on fossil energy, so electricity achievements do not by themselves establish comprehensive fossil-fuel replacement.

target: AG2’s claim that alternatives cannot provide firm, dispatchable supply at scale and therefore fossil fuels must remain the backstop.
objection: AG1 argues that the assumption is false because countries already achieve very high low-carbon electricity shares using dispatchable sources like hydropower and geothermal. This undermines the claim that fossil fuels are needed as a dependable backstop until alternatives become capable of firmness at scale.

target: AG1’s claim that fossil-fuel use can be effectively replaced by low-carbon energy without addressing all fossil-linked capital stock immediately.
objection: AG2 argues that fossil fuels are embedded in long-lived assets such as power plants, boilers, industrial equipment, vehicles, and fuel distribution systems. Since these assets cannot be displaced instantly, alternatives cannot effectively replace fossil fuels quickly enough to meet total demand without a bridge fuel.

target: AG2’s premise that alternatives cannot be scaled fast enough to displace fossil generation and fuel demand.
objection: AG1 counters that effective replacement does not require instant retirement of every fossil asset; what matters is displacing the fossil generation and fuel services that would otherwise meet demand. Once low-carbon capacity is scaled, fossil output falls even if some legacy assets remain.

target: AG1’s claim that dispatchable low-carbon generation can reduce fossil output enough to make natural gas unnecessary as a bridge.
objection: AG2 argues that the dispatch/merit-order logic still depends on firm capacity during variable renewable periods. Without sufficient firm low-carbon power or storage, fossil plants must remain online for reliability, so the claim that dispatch alone can largely displace fossil fuels is not justified.

target: AG2’s idea that effective replacement requires the immediate retirement of all fossil-linked assets and full elimination of fossil end-use equipment before alternatives count as replacing fossil fuels.
objection: AG1 objects that this is an overly strict definition of replacement. In practice, alternative generation can substitute for fossil services gradually by displacing fossil units in dispatch order and by reducing fossil use as electrification and low-carbon heat expand, even while some legacy equipment remains.

target: AG1’s assumption that fossil end-use capital can be sidelined without rapid replacement and still count as effective replacement.
objection: AG2 argues that fossil fuels are not just marginal electricity generation but also a major part of transportation and heat. Because those end uses rely on durable equipment and fuel systems, low-carbon electricity growth does not automatically eliminate fossil demand, so fossil fuels continue to provide essential energy services until those sectors are transformed.

target: AG2’s claim that effective replacement requires immediate retirement of every fossil asset and that such strict replacement is necessary to count as success.
objection: AG1 reiterates that replacement can be effective even if some fossil assets remain installed. Countries with very high renewable electricity shares demonstrate that fossil generation can be largely displaced in operation, so natural gas is not a logically necessary bridge merely because legacy assets still exist.

target: AG1’s reliance on nuclear as the firm low-carbon source that would make fossil displacement realistic.
objection: AG2 argues that nuclear is too dangerous and unreliable to serve as a dependable replacement pathway. Accidents like Fukushima can erase the practical carbon-free benefit and create major disruption, so nuclear cannot be assumed to provide the firm low-carbon capacity needed for effective fossil-fuel replacement.
